title: GST_122 — End of Semester Objective Exam
guideTitle: GST_122 — Communication in English Language II

questions.q: Which of the following is the course's definition of writing?
options: The ability to comprehend, interpret, and analyse written text.
The ability to articulate thoughts, ideas, and information coherently and effectively.
The capacity to convey thoughts, information, and emotions through written language.
The ability to understand, interpret, and respond to spoken language.
questions.why: Why C is right: the course alone among the four skills calls writing a capacity, and writing alone is defined as conveying emotions. Why the others are wrong: A is the definition of reading, swapped in because both skills concern written language · B is the definition of speaking · D is the definition of listening.

questions.q: Three of the four language skills are defined as an "ability". Which one does the course define as a "capacity"?
questions.why: Why A is right: the course's wording is "the capacity to convey thoughts, information, and emotions through written language". Why the others are wrong: B is defined as the ability to comprehend, interpret and analyse written text · C is defined as the ability to understand, interpret and respond to spoken language · D is defined as the ability to articulate thoughts, ideas and information.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six things the course says effective speaking includes?
questions.why: Why D is right: eye contact belongs to Week 10's physical aspects of public speaking and Week 12's active-listening techniques, not to Week 1's six elements of effective speaking. Why the others are wrong: A is the fourth of the six · B is the fifth of the six · C is the second of the six.

questions.q: According to the course, hearing is:
options: active and voluntary, requiring conscious effort
full engagement with the speaker's message
questions.why: Why B is right: the course states that hearing is passive and involuntary, while listening is active and voluntary, requiring conscious effort to interpret and understand. Why the others are wrong: A is the course's description of listening, not of hearing · C is the definition of passive listening, which is contrasted with active listening, not with hearing · D is the definition of active listening.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the four writing styles named in Week 1?
questions.why: Why B is right: the four writing styles are persuasive, descriptive, narrative and expository. Why the others are wrong: A is one of the eleven writing strategies of Week 4, not one of the four styles · C is one of the eleven writing strategies of Week 4 · D is one of the eleven writing strategies of Week 4.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four key takeaways from the passage "The Dangers of Faking Mental Health Issues"?
questions.why: Why D is right: the four named takeaways are Undermining Legitimacy, Obstructing Access to Support, Misallocation of Resources, and Honesty and Understanding. Why the others are wrong: A is the third named takeaway · B is the second named takeaway · C is the fourth named takeaway.

questions.q: Listening to background music while cooking, as against listening during a lecture, is the course's example of:
questions.why: Why A is right: the course's stated example is "active listening during a lecture versus passive listening to background music". Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because hearing is the involuntary reception of sound and is contrasted with listening, not with active listening; the course uses this example for the active/passive pair · C is a Week 11 listening strategy concerned with the speaker's emotions · D is not a term the course uses.

questions.q: Kermode's Speak So Your Audience Will Listen is given in the course as the reference for which skill?
questions.why: Why C is right: the Week 1 reference list pairs Kermode with public speaking, Pinker with language and Dehaene with reading. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because Dehaene's Reading in the Brain is the reference given for reading · B is wrong because Adler's How to Speak, How to Listen is the Week 11 reference for listening · D is wrong because no writing reference is given in the Week 1 list.

questions.q: The course defines semiotics as:
options: the study of signs and symbols, their interpretation, and their role in communication
the study of the literal meanings that words carry independently of culture
the study of how sentences are constructed from subjects, predicates and objects
the study of the cultural and emotional associations that words acquire
questions.why: Why A is right: this is the course's wording, given in the Week 8 vocabulary list and applied in Week 2. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because this describes denotation, which is one kind of meaning, not the field of semiotics · C is wrong because this describes syntax, of which the sentence is said to be an aspect · D is wrong because this describes connotation rather than semiotics.

questions.q: "Home" and "house" both name a place where a person lives, but "home" also suggests warmth, safety and belonging. The warmth-safety-belonging element is the word's:
questions.why: Why C is right: connotative meaning is the implied or suggested meaning, carrying the cultural and emotional aspects of communication. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because denotative meaning is the literal meaning, which the two words share · B is a Week 7 reading term for what is directly stated in a text · D is a Week 7 reading term for suggested information in a text, not for the associations carried by a single word.

questions.q: The course names two potential sources of confusion in communication. They are:
questions.why: Why B is right: these are the two named in the Week 2 summary, to be avoided for clarity. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because homograph is a standard term but is not used in the course; only homophones are named · C is wrong because connotation is a kind of meaning, not one of the two named sources of confusion · D is wrong because jargon is mentioned only in Week 9's guideline about speaking clearly.

questions.q:
The sentence below is the course's example of:
> The manager told the supervisor that he would be promoted.
questions.why: Why D is right: the sentence carries more than one meaning because the pronoun "he" can refer to either party, which is the course's definition of ambiguity. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because homophones are words that sound alike but differ in meaning and spelling; this is a whole-sentence problem, not a word-level one · B is wrong because no implied or cultural association is at issue here · C is wrong because semiotics concerns signs and symbols beyond language.

questions.q: According to James Pennebaker, function words account for less than one-tenth of 1 percent of your vocabulary but make up almost what share of the words you actually use?
questions.why: Why D is right: the quoted figure is "almost 60 percent of the words you use". Why the others are wrong: A is an understatement produced by confusing the two Pennebaker figures · B is wrong because no figure of this size appears in the course · C is an overstatement; the course's figure is almost 60 percent.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT given by the course as another name for function words?
questions.why: Why B is right: lexical words is the course's alternative name for CONTENT words, not function words. Why the others are wrong: A is the third of the seven alternative names · C is the sixth of the seven alternative names · D is the seventh of the seven alternative names.

questions.q: Which part of speech does the course place among the function-word classes?
questions.why: Why C is right: the five function-word classes are conjunctions, auxiliary/helping verbs, prepositions, articles and pronouns. Why the others are wrong: A is one of the four content-word classes · B is one of the four content-word classes · D is one of the four content-word classes.

questions.q: In the sentence "She has eaten the mango", the course would classify "has" and "eaten" respectively as:
options: a function word and a content word
a content word and a function word
questions.why: Why A is right: "has" is an auxiliary supporting the main verb, so it is a function word; "eaten" is the lexical verb carrying the meaning, so it is a content word. Why the others are wrong: B is the classification reversed; the helper is the function word · C is wrong because verbs are a content class, but auxiliaries are listed separately as function words · D is wrong because "eaten" is the main verb and carries the meaning of the sentence.

questions.q: In "She BOUGHT a NEW CAR at the MARKET", the capitalised words are the stressed ones. The course explains this by the rule that:
options: function words are stressed and content words are not
content words are stressed and function words are not
only nouns are stressed in English
the last word of every phrase is stressed
questions.why: Why B is right: the course states that emphasis in English conversation is placed on content words, while function words remain non-stressed. Why the others are wrong: A is the rule reversed · C is wrong because the stressed words here include a verb and an adjective as well as nouns · D is not a rule the course gives.

questions.q: For a sentence to be deemed complete, the course says it must possess:
options: a noun or pronoun (subject) and a verb (predicate)
an independent clause and a dependent clause
a subject, a verb and a complement
questions.why: Why A is right: this is the course's wording: two important parts of speech, a noun or pronoun as subject and a verb as predicate. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because the object is optional; the course names the predicate, not the object · C is wrong because that describes a complex sentence, not the minimum for any sentence · D is wrong because the complement is not part of the course's requirement.

questions.q: Describing a sentence by its purpose is describing it by its:
questions.why: Why C is right: the course says that when a sentence is described by its function, it is being described by its purpose. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because structure describes how a sentence is made up of parts such as subjects, predicates and objects · B is wrong because the course calls the sentence an aspect of syntax, but syntax is not one of the two ways of analysing it · D is a standard grammatical term, but not one the course uses.

questions.q:
Classify the sentence below by structure.
> Although it was raining, they decided to go for a walk, and they took umbrellas just in case.
questions.why: Why D is right: it has two independent clauses ("they decided to go for a walk" and "they took umbrellas just in case") plus one dependent clause ("Although it was raining"). Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because a complex sentence has only one independent clause; there are two here · B is wrong because a compound sentence has no dependent clause; "Although it was raining" is one · C is wrong because a simple sentence has exactly one clause.

questions.q:
Classify the sentence below by structure.
> She loves to read; he prefers to watch movies.
questions.why: Why C is right: two independent clauses joined by a semicolon; the course states that a compound sentence may be formed with a semicolon and no conjunction at all. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because there are two complete clauses, not one · B is wrong because neither clause is dependent on the other · D is wrong because a compound-complex sentence needs at least one dependent clause.

questions.q: What distinguishes a compound sentence from a complex one?
options: A compound sentence is built with subordinating conjunctions, while a complex one is built with coordinating conjunctions.
A compound sentence contains a dependent clause, whereas a complex sentence contains none at all.
A compound sentence is longer than a complex one.
A compound sentence joins clauses of equal rank; a complex one joins an independent clause to a dependent clause.
questions.why: Why D is right: compound sentences coordinate clauses that could each stand alone, while complex sentences subordinate one clause to another. Why the others are wrong: A is the two conjunction types swapped: coordinating for compound, subordinating for complex · B is exactly the reverse of the definitions · C is wrong because length has nothing to do with the classification, which counts clauses.

questions.q: Besides declarative, imperative, interrogative and exclamatory, the course adds a fifth category of sentence. It is:
questions.why: Why A is right: the course adds conditional sentences, also known as "if" sentences, which express conditions and their likely results. Why the others are wrong: B is a standard grammatical term the course never uses · C is a mood, not one of the course's sentence categories · D is wrong because the course mentions rhetorical questions only under the question mark.

questions.q: "Please pass the salt" and "The sun rises in the east" both end in a full stop. The first is imperative because it:
options: states a fact about the world
questions.why: Why B is right: imperative sentences give commands, instructions or requests; only purpose separates them from declaratives, since both end in a full stop. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because that is what a declarative sentence does · C is wrong because it begins with "Please", and word order is not the course's test · D is wrong because politeness is a matter of tone, not of sentence function.

questions.q: Concord is best defined as:
options: a set of rules governing agreement between elements in a sentence
the arrangement of words into phrases and clauses within a sentence
the correct use of punctuation to clarify the meaning of a sentence
the matching of tone and style to the audience a writer has in mind
questions.why: Why A is right: the course adds that concord ensures linguistic harmony and fosters credibility in written and spoken language. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because that is syntax; concord is specifically about agreement, not arrangement · C is wrong because that is the course's account of punctuation · D is wrong because that is Week 4's point about audience awareness.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: "Neither the lecturer nor the students ___ available."
questions.why: Why B is right: the Rule of Proximity Agreement requires the verb to align with the closest subject, and the closest subject here is the plural "students". Why the others are wrong: A is correct only if the singular "lecturer" stood nearest the verb, as in "Neither the students nor the lecturer is available" · C is wrong because it is wrong in number for the same reason as "is", and wrong in tense for the given frame · D is singular, so it clashes with the nearest subject.

questions.q: Which of the following sentences applies the course's concord rules correctly?
options: The bag of apples are heavy.
Neither the students nor the lecturer are available.
Either the boys or the girl are singing.
The bag of apples is heavy.
questions.why: Why D is right: the subject is "bag", which is singular; "of apples" is a prepositional phrase, and the nearest noun is not always the subject. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because it over-applies proximity by agreeing with the nearest noun instead of the actual subject · B is wrong because it breaks proximity agreement: the nearest subject is the singular "lecturer", so the verb should be "is" · C is wrong because it breaks proximity agreement: the nearest subject is the singular "girl", so the verb should be "is".

questions.q:
The pair of sentences below is the course's illustration of which use of punctuation?
> "Let's eat, Grandma." / "Let's eat Grandma."
questions.why: Why C is right: the course places the Grandma pair under "Changing the Meaning", where the comma decides who is being eaten. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because the course reserves this heading for "I like cooking, my family, and pets", where a list is at stake · B is wrong because the course's example of emphasis is "We won the game!" against "We won the game." · D is wrong because the course's example of nuance is "I appreciate your help." against "I appreciate your help!".

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five uses the course gives for the comma?
options: Setting off introductory phrases and clauses at the start of a sentence
Separating adjectives that modify the same noun
Setting off non-essential or parenthetical information
Joining two independent clauses that have no conjunction between them
questions.why: Why D is right: that is the semicolon's first named use; a comma joins independent clauses only when a coordinating conjunction is present. Why the others are wrong: A is the second of the five comma uses · B is the third of the five comma uses · C is the fifth of the five comma uses.

questions.q: Which punctuation mark does the course describe as introducing a list, an explanation or a quotation?
questions.why: Why C is right: the colon's three named uses are introducing a list, introducing an explanation and introducing a quotation; the colon announces what follows. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because the semicolon balances two things of equal weight rather than introducing something · B is wrong because the dash emphasises, replaces parentheses or creates a dramatic pause · D is wrong because the comma separates and sets off; it does not introduce.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the three named uses of the semicolon?
options: Introducing an explanation that elaborates on the preceding statement
Separating items in a list when the items themselves contain commas
Indicating words omitted from a quotation
questions.why: Why B is right: this is the semicolon's "super-comma" use, as in "London, UK; Berlin, Germany; and Paris, France". Why the others are wrong: A is one of the colon's three uses · C is one of the comma's five uses · D is the ellipsis's first named use.

questions.q: Which form correctly shows essays belonging to several students?
questions.why: Why A is right: for a plural noun already ending in -s, the apostrophe follows the -s; this is the course's plural-possession use. Why the others are wrong: B is singular possession: the essays of one student · C is a plural with no possessive marking at all · D is an incorrect doubling; the plural -s is not repeated.

questions.q: An editor inserts a clarifying word inside a direct quotation, as in "I look forward to [the] challenge." The inserted word is enclosed in:
questions.why: Why B is right: brackets are used to add information or editorial comment inside someone else's quoted words. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because round brackets enclose your own supplementary information, acronyms or citations, not insertions into a quotation · C is wrong because these mark the quotation itself, not an editorial insertion within it · D is wrong because an ellipsis marks words left out, not words added.

questions.q: According to the course, an em dash is:
options: shorter than an en dash and used for joining the parts of compound words
the same length as a hyphen but placed between clauses
longer than an en dash and often used in place of parentheses or commas
used only to break a word at the end of a printed line
questions.why: Why C is right: the course states this distinction directly, and gives the em dash the jobs of emphasising, replacing parentheses and creating a dramatic pause. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because joining compound words is the hyphen's job, and the em dash is the longer mark · B is wrong because it confuses the dash with the hyphen, which is the short joining mark · D is wrong because breaking words at a line end is a named use of the hyphen.

questions.q: A market sign reads: Fresh "Fish". On the course's account of quotation marks, the marks here signal:
options: the title of a short work
questions.why: Why D is right: the third named use of quotation marks is sarcastic or ironic, as in his so-called "expertise"; the sign ends up denying that the fish is really fish. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because quotation marks are not an emphasis device; that job belongs to the exclamation point or the dash · B is wrong because nobody is being quoted on the sign · C is wrong because that use covers articles, short stories and chapters.

questions.q: The course says that accounts of what makes a good paragraph vary, but that one component remains constant. Which is it?
questions.why: Why A is right: the course states outright that one component remains constant, the topic sentence, and that five paragraphs require five topic sentences. Why the others are wrong: B is one of the four components listed, but not the one the course calls constant · C is one of the four components listed, but not the constant one · D is one of the four components listed, but not the constant one.

questions.q: A paragraph in which every sentence is about the same subject, but the sentences do not lead from one to the next, lacks:
questions.why: Why A is right: coherence is a matter of orderly, logically connected ideas held together by cohesive links such as conjunctions and pronouns; the course's morning-run example has exactly this fault. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because unity means a single central theme with no digression, and that condition is already met here · C is wrong because nothing in the description says the main idea is unstated · D is wrong because supporting sentences add details to the topic sentence; the problem here is the joins, not the content.

questions.q: Which group contains only transition words of contrast?
options: Similarly, Likewise, In the same way
questions.why: Why D is right: these are the first three items in the course's Contrast column. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because these belong to the Cause and Effect column · B is wrong because these belong to the Comparison column · C is wrong because these belong to the Emphasis column.

questions.q: An essay that sets out, step by step, how a report is written uses which of the eleven writing strategies?
questions.why: Why C is right: process analysis explains how something is done, step by step, and the course's own example for it is "How to write a report". Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because it arranges material by time, such as the history of the university, rather than by procedure · B is wrong because it explains without arguing, but the course reserves the step-by-step procedure for process analysis · D is wrong because it tells a story in sequence, such as an account of registration week.

questions.q: The course names the stages of the writing process as:
questions.why: Why B is right: the course's wording is "cohesive sets of activities encompassing pre-writing, during-writing, and post-writing stages". Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because editing is one post-writing activity among ten, not a stage · C is wrong because publishing is the tenth post-writing activity, not a stage · D is wrong because these are single activities drawn from the pre-writing and post-writing lists.

questions.q: The course compares pre-writing to an architect planning a structure. To what does it compare post-writing?
questions.why: Why C is right: post-writing is likened to polishing a gem for clarity and shine. Why the others are wrong: A is the course's analogy for report crafting · B is the course's second analogy for letter writing · D is the course's analogy for word formation processes.

questions.q: A filmmaker plans the sequence of scenes in a film visually. Which pre-writing activity is this?
questions.why: Why B is right: storyboarding organises narrative structure visually, and the filmmaker is the course's own example for it. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because the course's example for mind mapping is a student branching the pros and cons of social media · C is wrong because the course's example for outlining is a speaker preparing key points and evidence · D is wrong because the course's example for clustering is a poet associating words around a central theme.

questions.q: Which three divergent thinking methods does the course name in its pre-writing objectives?
options: Research, outlining, identifying audience and purpose
questions.why: Why A is right: these three are named together as the divergent thinking techniques used in brainstorming. Why the others are wrong: B is three pre-writing activities, but the course does not call them divergent thinking · C is three pre-writing activities that are not the named divergent methods · D is a set of planning and information-gathering activities, not divergent thinking.

questions.q: Catching typographical errors, misspellings and punctuation mistakes is the work of:
questions.why: Why D is right: proofreading is the last, surface-level pass; the course names typographical errors, misspellings and punctuation mistakes as its targets. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because revision reworks content and structure, such as reorganising paragraphs · B is wrong because editing fixes grammar, sentence structure and consistency of style · C is wrong because peer review is an exchange of drafts for feedback on clarity and argument.

questions.q: Who is credited in the course with the claim that learning often starts in your hand, travels up your arm, and lands in your brain?
questions.why: Why D is right: the Week 4 summary attributes this analogy to Bruce Edward. Why the others are wrong: A is cited for the two statistics about function words · B is cited for The Language Instinct as the Week 1 reference on language · C is cited for the grammar workbooks used as the concord references.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the ten post-writing activities?
questions.why: Why A is right: identifying audience and purpose is the sixth of the ten PRE-writing activities. Why the others are wrong: B is the seventh post-writing activity · C is the eighth post-writing activity · D is the third post-writing activity.

questions.q: Which of the following is the course's definition of a report?
options: A condensed version of a larger text, highlighting the main ideas and key points.
A formal document presenting information, analysis, findings and conclusions on a specific topic.
A written message addressed to a specific person or group.
The systematic investigation of materials and sources in order to establish facts and reach conclusions.
questions.why: Why B is right: the course adds that a report follows a structured format and is used in academic, business and professional settings. Why the others are wrong: A is the definition of a summary · C is the definition of a letter · D is the Week 8 vocabulary definition of research.

questions.q: The course names five sections of a report. They are:
questions.why: Why C is right: these are the sections the course lists both in its definition of a report and in the worked sample on global poverty. Why the others are wrong: A is a general essay skeleton; references and appendices are a report step, not one of the five sections · B is wrong because these are steps in writing a report, not sections appearing on the page · D is a standard scientific-paper layout that the course does not use.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five key parts of a letter?
questions.why: Why B is right: choosing the right format is the second STEP in writing a letter; the five parts are the greeting, opening sentence, purpose, closing and signature. Why the others are wrong: A is the second of the five key parts · C is the third of the five key parts · D is the fifth of the five key parts.

questions.q: How many steps to writing a letter, and how many key parts of a letter, does the course give?
questions.why: Why D is right: the steps are a procedure of nine, and the parts are an anatomy of five. Why the others are wrong: A is the two figures reversed · B is wrong because eight is the number of steps for writing a summary · C is wrong because eleven is the number of steps for writing a report.

questions.q: Which step in writing a summary requires you to put the key points into your own words?
questions.why: Why C is right: the course's wording for this step is "summarise the key points in your own words, focusing on brevity and clarity". Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because it identifies the supporting details and examples; nothing is rewritten yet · B is wrong because it retains the logical order of the original text · D is wrong because it omits minor details unless they are crucial.

questions.q: A student produces a "summary" by copying whole sentences out of the original and rearranging them. Which two summary steps has the student broken?
options: Read the Text Carefully and Check for Coherence
Highlight Key Points and Review and Revise
Eliminate Unnecessary Details and Review and Revise
questions.why: Why A is right: condensing requires your own words, which copying breaks, and maintaining structure requires the original's logical order, which rearranging breaks. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because nothing in the description says the text was misread or that the result fails to flow · C is wrong because identifying key points and editing at the end are not what copying and rearranging violate · D is wrong because the fault described is not the retention of minor details.

questions.q: Which step in writing a report does the course qualify with the words "if applicable"?
questions.why: Why A is right: the eighth step is given as "Make Recommendations (if applicable)", and the qualifier should be reproduced. Why the others are wrong: B is given without qualification, and required for transparency and reliability · C is given without qualification as the tenth step · D is given without qualification as the ninth step.

questions.q: Steps 7 and 8 in writing a letter are "Closing" and "Closing Salutation". What distinguishes them?
options: The Closing is the sign-off phrase and signature; the Closing Salutation is the letter's final paragraph.
They are two names the course gives to a single step.
The Closing is the final paragraph; the Closing Salutation is the closing phrase and signature.
The Closing ends an informal letter; the Closing Salutation ends a formal one.
questions.why: Why C is right: the Closing summarises and expresses gratitude or goodwill, while the Closing Salutation is the sign-off, such as "Yours sincerely", plus the signature. Why the others are wrong: A is the two steps swapped · B is wrong because the course lists them as separate numbered steps · D is wrong because the distinction is not one of register; both appear in the same letter.

questions.q: SQ3R stands for:
questions.why: Why D is right: S is Survey, Q is Question and the three Rs are Read, Recite and Review, in that order. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because they are plausible synonyms, but none of these five is the course's term · B is wrong because it substitutes Record for Recite, which loses the spoken step · C is wrong because it substitutes Skim for Survey and Reflect for Review.

questions.q: In which SQ3R step do you generate questions rather than answer them?
questions.why: Why B is right: the course is explicit: "This is where you start asking questions, not answering the questions from the passage". Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because the survey scans headings, subheadings and images for an overview · C is wrong because reading is where the questions you generated get answered · D is wrong because reciting explains key points aloud after reading.

questions.q: The course gives two goals for the Read stage. One is to read to answer the questions you generated. The other is:
options: to create summaries, outlines or notes
to explain the key points and concepts aloud
to engage with the material and gain a fuller understanding
to note down the headings, subheadings and images you surveyed
questions.why: Why C is right: these are the two goals the course states for the Read phase. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because that is what happens in the Review step · B is wrong because that is the Recite step · D is wrong because that is the Survey step.

questions.q: What distinguishes Recite from Review?
options: Recite explains the key points aloud; Review creates summaries, outlines or notes.
Recite creates the written summaries and outlines; Review explains the key points aloud.
Recite comes before reading; Review comes after it.
Recite is done silently; Review is done aloud.
questions.why: Why A is right: reciting is spoken and immediate, while reviewing is written and aimed at long-term retention and recall in exams. Why the others are wrong: B is the two steps swapped · C is wrong because both follow the Read step; the order is Read, Recite, Review · D is wrong because the course's instruction for Recite is "Vocalise your thoughts!".

questions.q: What does the course say about the status of SQ3R?
options: It is the definition of a reading strategy.
It is one reading strategy among several.
questions.why: Why B is right: the course defines reading strategies in general and then adds that "SQ3R happens to be one of these strategies". Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because it confuses one named method with the general category it belongs to · C is wrong because the note-taking method named in the course is Cornell · D is wrong because SQ3R is a reading strategy, not part of the writing process.

questions.q:
In the sentence below, a reader who does not know the word "vituperative" works out that it means bitterly abusive. Which reading strategy has the reader used?
> The senator's remarks were so vituperative that three delegates walked out.
questions.why: Why D is right: context clues are hints within a text that help the reader infer the meaning of an unfamiliar word, which is exactly what the walk-out supplies. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because inference draws a logical conclusion about the situation, not about the meaning of an unknown word · B is wrong because implicit meaning concerns unspoken information in the text, not vocabulary · C is wrong because no separation of verifiable fact from subjective opinion is involved.

questions.q:
The sentence below never states that it is raining, yet the reader knows that it is. That meaning is:
> She came in shaking the rain off her umbrella.
questions.why: Why D is right: implicit meaning is unspoken or suggested information, which requires the reader to infer. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because explicit meaning is directly stated in the text and requires no inference · B is wrong because denotation is the literal meaning of a word, not information suggested by a sentence · C is wrong because connotation is the cultural or emotional association of a word.

questions.q: "Nigeria has 36 states" and "Nigeria has too many states" differ in that the second is:
questions.why: Why B is right: the course's critical-thinking strategy separates objective, verifiable facts from subjective opinions, and "too many" cannot be verified. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because an inference is a logical conclusion drawn from explicit details plus background knowledge, and can be defended · C is wrong because nothing is being suggested without being said; the judgement is stated openly · D is wrong because the sentence has only one reading.

questions.q: Vocabulary expansion is defined by the course as:
options: the process of increasing one's repertoire of words and expressions in a language
the vocabulary of a person, language or branch of knowledge
the ability to infer the meanings of unfamiliar words from their surroundings
the study of the origins and histories of words
questions.why: Why A is right: the course adds that it contributes to cognitive abilities, academic success and overall language proficiency. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because that is the course's definition of a lexicon, the thing expanded, not the process · C is wrong because that describes the use of context clues, a Week 7 reading strategy · D is wrong because etymology, which the course does not teach.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four strategies for vocabulary expansion?
options: Using dictionaries, thesauruses and language-learning apps
Learning a fixed number of new words by heart each day
Playing word games and taking part in language-related activities
questions.why: Why C is right: the four strategies are reading widely, using vocabulary-building tools, engaging in conversation and debate, and playing word games; rote quotas are not among them. Why the others are wrong: A is the first of the four strategies · B is the second strategy, the vocabulary-building tools · D is the fourth strategy.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven benefits of vocabulary expansion?
questions.why: Why A is right: the seven benefits are communication skills, intellectual growth, academic achievement, professional success, cultural competence, lifelong learning, and reading and writing proficiency. Why the others are wrong: B is the fifth of the seven benefits · C is the sixth of the seven benefits · D is the fourth of the seven benefits.

questions.q: "Brunch" is the course's example of which word formation process?
questions.why: Why D is right: blending combines parts of words, here the start of breakfast and the end of lunch. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because compounding merges whole words, as in raincoat · B is wrong because derivation adds a derivational suffix, as in teacher · C is wrong because conversion changes a word's grammatical category without any affix, as in email used as a verb.

questions.q: What distinguishes compounding from blending?
options: Compounding uses prefixes; blending uses suffixes.
Compounding joins whole words; blending joins parts of words.
Compounding changes a word's class; blending does not.
Compounding forms acronyms; blending forms abbreviations.
questions.why: Why B is right: raincoat is rain plus coat, both entire; brunch takes only a fragment from each source word. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because prefixes and suffixes belong to affixation, not to either of these · C is wrong because changing word class without an affix is conversion · D is wrong because acronyms take initial letters, and the course does not teach abbreviation as a process.

questions.q: Using the noun "email" as a verb, with nothing added to the word, is an example of:
questions.why: Why C is right: conversion alters a word's grammatical category without affixes. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because derivation changes the word by adding a derivational suffix · B is wrong because affixation attaches a prefix or suffix, and nothing is attached here · D is wrong because borrowing introduces a word from another language, as with sushi.

questions.q: The course gives "teacher" as its example of which word formation process?
questions.why: Why C is right: derivation adds a derivational suffix to create a new word, and teacher is the course's example. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because affixation is illustrated in the course by unadulterated and correctly · B is wrong because compounding is illustrated by raincoat · D is wrong because conversion is illustrated by email used as a verb, with no affix added.

questions.q: Which academic term means thinking about one's own thinking processes, including awareness of one's cognitive abilities?
questions.why: Why B is right: this is the course's definition of metacognition, one of the ten terms singled out in the crossword. Why the others are wrong: A is the branch of philosophy concerned with the nature, origin and scope of knowledge · C is critical explanation or interpretation, especially of a text · D is the method and practice of teaching.

questions.q: Which term names the practice of emphasising moral or educational messages in literature, art or teaching?
questions.why: Why D is right: didacticism is the practice; the course lists it separately from the adjective didactic. Why the others are wrong: A is the adjective, describing something intended to instruct or teach · B is the method and practice of teaching as an academic subject · C is the skill of clear and expressive speech, especially public speaking.

questions.q: Speaking prompts are defined by the course as:
options: questions or statements designed to elicit a spoken response
guidelines for organising and delivering a speech
the opening remarks that set the tone of a presentation
cues by which an audience signals attention to a speaker
questions.why: Why A is right: the course adds that they serve as a stimulus to initiate and guide verbal communication in interviews, discussions and public speaking. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because that describes the thirteen guidelines for responding to prompts, not the prompts themselves · C is wrong because an introduction is one guideline for responding, not a definition of a prompt · D is wrong because audience cues belong to the discussion of non-verbal affirmations in Week 12.

questions.q: The course gives nine items under one Week 9 heading and thirteen under another. The thirteen are:
options: the reasons speaking prompts are important
the guidelines for responding to speaking prompts
questions.why: Why B is right: the nine say why prompts matter; the thirteen say how to answer one. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because that is the list of nine · C is wrong because the course names three benefits of active listening, in Week 12 · D is wrong because the course names four elements of delivery, in Week 10.

questions.q: "Consider different angles or counterarguments where they apply" is which of the guidelines for responding to a speaking prompt?
questions.why: Why A is right: the guideline named Balance asks for a balanced perspective that considers different angles or counterarguments. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because it asks for sufficient detail to address the prompt fully · C is wrong because it warns against veering off into unrelated tangents · D is wrong because it asks you to adjust register, as between an academic and a casual setting.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the thirteen guidelines for responding to a speaking prompt?
questions.why: Why D is right: building confidence is the seventh reason speaking prompts are IMPORTANT, not one of the guidelines for answering one. Why the others are wrong: A is the thirteenth guideline · B is the twelfth guideline · C is the second guideline.

questions.q: In linguistics, the course defines stress as:
options: the rise and fall of the voice across a whole utterance, marking it out as a question or a statement
the speed and rhythm at which a speaker delivers a sentence
the emphasis on a particular syllable or segment within a word, phrase or sentence during speech
the pause a speaker leaves between clauses
questions.why: Why C is right: this is the course's exact wording, and it covers both word stress and sentence stress. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because that describes intonation, which the course never defines · B is wrong because pace is mentioned under speaking clearly, not as the definition of stress · D is wrong because pauses are one of the four elements of delivery in Week 10.

questions.q:
In the course's example sentence below, stressing the word "you" implies:
> I didn't say you should bring coffee.
options: that the speaker denies saying it at all
that it was optional rather than obligatory
that something other than coffee should be brought
that somebody else should bring it
questions.why: Why D is right: the course's table gives "somebody else should bring it" as the reading produced by stressing you. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because that is the reading produced by stressing didn't · B is wrong because that is the reading produced by stressing should · C is wrong because that is the reading produced by stressing coffee.

questions.q: PREsent (a gift) as against preSENT (to give) is an illustration of:
questions.why: Why C is right: word stress concerns which syllable within a word is emphasised, and moving it here changes both class and meaning. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because sentence stress concerns which word within a sentence is emphasised · B is a term the course does not teach · D is clarity of articulation, mentioned only under speaking clearly and concisely.

questions.q: Inductive reasoning is a form of reasoning in which the conclusion is:
options: likely or probable, but not certain, given the premises
necessarily true if the premises on which it rests are true
drawn from two given or assumed propositions
guaranteed once the argument is valid
questions.why: Why A is right: the course's definition; induction looks for patterns in order to draw a conclusion or make a generalisation. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because that is the definition of deductive reasoning · C is wrong because that is the definition of a syllogism, a deductive form · D is wrong because validity and guaranteed conclusions belong to deduction.

questions.q: In which directions do the two kinds of reasoning run?
options: Induction moves from general to specific; deduction from specific to general.
Induction moves from specific to general; deduction from general to specific.
Both move from general premises to specific conclusions.
Both move from specific observations to general conclusions.
questions.why: Why B is right: Week 12 states this outright: deduction draws specific conclusions from general premises, and induction starts with specific observations to make broader generalisations. Why the others are wrong: A is the two directions swapped, the commonest error on this pair · C is wrong because that describes deduction alone · D is wrong because that describes induction alone.

questions.q: A village wishes to estimate its population for the next 15 years. Which reasoning is appropriate, and why?
options: Inductive, because it projects a probable future from observed past patterns
Deductive, because the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises
Deductive, because the estimate rests on statistical data
Inductive, because the premises are certainly true
questions.why: Why A is right: the course's own answer; the estimate is a probable conclusion drawn from a pattern, not a certainty derived from a general rule. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because no general rule is being applied to a particular case, and no such projection is certain · C is wrong because statistical reasoning is a type of INDUCTIVE reasoning, not a mark of deduction · D is the right label with the wrong reason; induction is defined by a probable conclusion, not by certain premises.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three types of inductive reasoning the course discusses with examples?
questions.why: Why B is right: abductive reasoning is one of four further types the course only names and tells you to find out more about; the three taught are generalisation, analogical reasoning and statistical reasoning. Why the others are wrong: A is the first of the three taught, with the sunglasses-and-hats example · C is the second of the three taught, with the cat-breed example · D is the third of the three taught, with the 70 percent election example.

questions.q: "Cats are known to be good hunters; this new breed shares their characteristics; so it is likely to be a good hunter too." This is:
questions.why: Why C is right: analogical reasoning draws a conclusion about one thing from its similarities to another. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because statistical reasoning argues from data or probability, and there are no figures here · B is wrong because generalisation makes a broad statement about a group from many observations, not a claim about one case from similarity · D is one of the four types the course only names, and no cause is being claimed.

questions.q: Which pattern is Modus Tollens?
options: If A, then B; A; therefore, B
If A, then B; Not A; therefore, Not B
All A are B; C is an A; therefore, C is a B
If A, then B; Not B; therefore, Not A
questions.why: Why D is right: Modus Tollens denies the consequent and concludes by denying the antecedent. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because that is Modus Ponens, which affirms the antecedent · B is wrong because it denies the antecedent, which is not a valid form and is not in the course · C is wrong because that is the categorical syllogism, which works on categories rather than a conditional.

questions.q:
The argument below is:
> All cats can fly. Tom is a cat. Therefore, Tom can fly.
questions.why: Why B is right: the conclusion follows logically from the premises, which makes it valid; the first premise is false, so it is not sound. Why the others are wrong: A is impossible on the course's definitions, since soundness requires validity · C is wrong because soundness also requires the premises to be true, and cats cannot fly · D is wrong because the form is impeccable; only the truth of the premise fails.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three limitations of inductive reasoning the course names?
questions.why: Why C is right: validity is a property of deductive arguments; the three limitations named are sampling bias, reliance on incomplete data and the potential for coincidental patterns. Why the others are wrong: A is the first named limitation · B is the second named limitation · D is the third named limitation.

questions.q: The four elements of delivery named in Week 10 are:
options: gestures, eye contact, stage utilisation and posture
diction, repetition, vocal variety and volume
questions.why: Why A is right: the course says these four contribute to the impact of a spoken message, surpassing the literal meaning of words. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because the first three are the physical aspects of public speaking, a different list, and posture is not in the course · C is wrong because the first three are the goals of a speech; entertainment is not among them · D is wrong because diction and repetition make up the language dimension, and vocal variety is a separate dimension.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six reasons the course gives for the importance of listening?
questions.why: Why D is right: problem solving is one of the three benefits of ACTIVE listening in Week 12; the six reasons are effective communication, building relationships, conflict resolution, learning and growth, leadership effectiveness and avoiding miscommunication. Why the others are wrong: A is the fifth of the six reasons · B is the sixth of the six reasons · C is the second of the six reasons.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six listening strategies given in Week 11?
questions.why: Why D is right: maintaining eye contact is one of Week 12's active-listening techniques; Week 11's strategies are active listening, nonverbal communication, empathetic listening, paraphrasing, summarising and note-taking. Why the others are wrong: A is the third of the six strategies · B is the second of the six strategies · C is the sixth of the six strategies.

questions.q: Regular self-assessment to identify areas for improvement in one's listening is what the Week 11 case study calls:
questions.why: Why A is right: the case study adds Cultural Awareness and Reflective Practice as further headings, the second being regular self-assessment. Why the others are wrong: B is the other added heading, which concerns communication differences across cultures · C is a Week 8 vocabulary term for thinking about one's own thinking, not a listening heading · D is an evaluation of scholarly work by experts, or a post-writing exchange of drafts.

questions.q: Which of the following appears in the Week 11 list of practical listening strategies?
questions.why: Why C is right: the practical strategies are paraphrasing, summarising, asking clarifying questions, minimising distractions, avoiding prejudgment and note-taking. Why the others are wrong: A is a Week 12 active-listening technique; Week 11 names clarifying questions · B is a Week 12 active-listening technique · D is a Week 12 active-listening technique.

questions.q: The course says that when people feel heard and understood, what is strengthened?
questions.why: Why B is right: this appears under Building Relationships, where listening is also said to demonstrate empathy. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because these belong to Leadership Effectiveness, which concerns decisions and the work environment · C is wrong because these belong to note-taking and retention, in Week 12 · D is not a claim the course makes about listening.

questions.q: The course keeps three notions apart. Which statement states them correctly?
options: Hearing is a voluntary act, while listening happens without any conscious effort on the listener's part.
Hearing is simply another name for passive listening.
Hearing is involuntary; listening is voluntary; active listening adds full engagement.
Listening and active listening are two names for one process.
questions.why: Why C is right: hearing is passive and involuntary, listening is active and voluntary and needs conscious effort, and active listening is listening with full engagement signalled back to the speaker. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because it reverses the course's contrast; conscious effort is exactly what listening requires · B is wrong because passive listening is contrasted with active listening; hearing is contrasted with listening · D is wrong because the course treats passive listening as listening without deep comprehension, so the two are not identical.

questions.q: The three benefits of active listening named in Week 12 are:
options: conflict resolution, learning and growth, and leadership effectiveness
enhanced understanding, conflict resolution and problem solving
questions.why: Why D is right: the course gives exactly these three, of which enhanced understanding covers emotions, intentions and context as well as words. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because empathy and leadership belong to Week 11's six reasons listening matters · B is three of Week 11's six reasons, not Week 12's three benefits · C is wrong because these are listening strategies and techniques, not benefits.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six techniques for becoming a more active listener?
questions.why: Why B is right: avoiding prejudgment belongs to Week 11's practical listening strategies; the six techniques are maintaining eye contact, avoiding interruption, minimising distractions, asking open-ended questions, using verbal and non-verbal affirmations, and paraphrasing and summarising. Why the others are wrong: A is the second of the six techniques · C is the fourth of the six techniques · D is the fifth of the six techniques.

questions.q: The Cornell note-taking method divides the page into sections for:
questions.why: Why A is right: the three labelled regions are the Cue Column, the Note Taking Area and the Summaries band. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because these are separate note-taking tips, not the Cornell regions · C is wrong because the question-and-answer pattern belongs to SQ3R, not Cornell · D is not a division the course gives.

questions.q: The Week 12 structure for a logical presentation contains one element that an ordinary essay outline does not. Which is it?
questions.why: Why A is right: the five parts are introduction, main points, supporting evidence, counterarguments and conclusion, and the counterarguments echo the Balance guideline of Week 9. Why the others are wrong: B is wrong because an ordinary essay outline contains supporting material too · C is wrong because every essay outline ends in a conclusion · D is wrong because every essay outline has main points.

questions.q: What does the course say about how much of a lecture to write down?
options: Transcribe as much of the lecture as you possibly can, and then cut it down afterwards.
Write only headings and subheadings during the lecture.
Do not write verbatim; capture main ideas, key concepts and supporting evidence.
Write nothing during the lecture and reconstruct it afterwards.
questions.why: Why C is right: the course warns that transcribing everything causes information overload and that good notes are concise, not complete. Why the others are wrong: A is the opposite of the course's instruction, and the source of information overload · B is wrong because headings and subheadings are a way of organising notes, not a limit on their content · D is wrong because the Cornell method has you summarise shortly after the lecture, but the notes themselves are taken during it.

questions.q:
Which fault does the reasoning below commit?
> Two students from that department failed their examinations, so the department must be poorly taught.
questions.why: Why B is right: a broad conclusion is drawn from far too little evidence; the course names this as one of its two logical fallacies, and it is inductive reasoning done badly. Why the others are wrong: A is wrong because a strawman misrepresents an opponent's position and then attacks the weakened version · C is a type of inductive reasoning, not a fallacy, and no comparison is being drawn · D is a type of inductive reasoning based on data or probability, not a fallacy.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven steps of the presentation methodology?
questions.why: Why D is right: the seven steps are purpose definition, audience analysis, thesis establishment, logical structure implementation, deductive and inductive reasoning application, fallacy avoidance and source citation. Why the others are wrong: A is the second of the seven steps · B is the third of the seven steps · C is the sixth of the seven steps.
